title: What is known about 1RB1LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RB_0LA0LF_0LD1LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LE_0RC---_1RD0LA_1RE0RB_0LA0LF_0LD1LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is decoded as a base-4 odometer of walls (rules proved in Lean for every block length) and followed exactly to 101520 steps with no halt; what is left is whether the order in which blocks run out can ever produce a wall shape that halts.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 66,928 cells have been visited and 22,316 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.10×10<sup>19</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 51,038,671,798,159,773,055 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,013,776 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.056). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.468).

claims.title: The block structure
claims.text: At each visit of the left end the tape is a list of blocks of 100 separated by 1010; per visit the blocks lose 4, 12, 48, 192, 768 words (position by position), the last ones grow; no halt in 1.5·10<sup>10</sup> steps.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2.67×10<sup>128</sup> steps (region-memo accelerator)
claims.text: The region-memo accelerator tools/py/bbtools/regaccel.py ran the mirrored table (so that the counter is at the left end), with blocks of 3 cells, from blank tape for 1200 seconds and reached step 2.67×10128 without a halt. It keeps the tape run-length coded and, for each stretch of tape from the left end, a macro (the run until the head first leaves that stretch) computed by a symbolic run of the machine with the long runs as variables; a macro is used only when the linear inequalities its symbolic run assumed hold, otherwise the stretch is run again by the same recursion. So the run is exact, step count included. Check: 34 configurations of this run (every time the head faced blank tape on the right, up to 2×109 steps) agree cell for cell with a direct run (tools/py/regcheck.py). This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: The base-4 schedule
claims.text: In the turn points of the run, trips to the nearest wall repeat four times for each trip one wall further, as the digits of a base-4 counter.

claims.title: Shift rules, for any number of copies
claims.text: D runs right over the words 100 of a block (turning them into 001), F runs left over them (into 010), E runs left over separators 10, B runs right over 001; each for every number of copies and any tape around.

claims.title: The odometer rules, for every block length
claims.text: The four digit changes of a last wall (1010 → 0 → 1110 → 1), a carry through a wall 1 or a double wall into each digit, the four phases of a wall (1010)r+2 of r+2 merged walls for every r, the left end 10 → 00, and the new wall at the right end after an arrival in C: each a theorem steps n c = some c' for all block lengths and any tape to the left, with the exact step count (8 per word crossed plus a constant).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>1520</sup> steps (odometer macro)
claims.text: The exact macro of py/odometer/ (closed-form jumps over many trips when every wall is a known digit, otherwise one trip run cell by cell on a copy of the tape with long blocks cut down modulo 12, step count corrected per word) ran from blank tape to step 643559… (1521 digits) through 8,776 visits of the left end without a halt. Checked against the direct simulator c/rtrips.c: all trips of the cut-down runner to 3·109 steps, and the macro at every visit of the left end to 5·1010 steps, step counts included. This is a bounded run.

claims.title: The countdown, derived
claims.text: If no block runs out during a period, a period is 2·4<sup>k</sup> trips and the blocks change by −4, −12, −48, …, −12·4<sup>k−2</sup>, +12·4<sup>k−1</sup> (from the digit totals −3, +6 per cycle). A wall of r merged walls is again a digit with the same totals.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly at A>0 1 or D>1 1; no rule of the odometer does that, so a halt needs a wall shape or a run-out not met yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine builds blocks of the word 100 separated by walls, and the walls are the digits of a base-4 odometer that the head counts up one trip at a time; the blocks drain at rates 4, 12, 48, … per visit of the left end. This page runs the real machine, the odometer, and the exact countdown to 10<sup>1520</sup> steps.

facts.text: The digit changes of the odometer, in Lean for every block length.
The blocks' drain rates, level by level, now derived.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.056). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.468).
After 109 steps the tape spans 66,928 cells (50 left of the start, 49,870 right), with a density of 1s of 0.333.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Blocks that shrink at rates 4, 12, 48, …
html: At each visit of the left end (state E) the tape is a list of blocks of the word 100 separated by 1010 (0 is an empty block):

Down the columns, the first block loses 4 words per visit, the second 12, the third 48, then 192, 768. Between two such visits the head shuttles between the walls and the right end on a base-4 schedule: four short trips for each trip one wall further, and so on. Each trip moves a wall by one word.
The machine halts exactly when A reads a 0 followed by a 1 or D reads a 1 followed by a 1. Whether the way exhausted blocks are refilled ever produces that is the open question.

sections.heading: A base-4 odometer of walls
html: Look at the tape each time the head arrives back at the right end. It is always L an1 w1 an2 w2 … wk ank+1 1 D>1 0: blocks of the word a = 100 separated by walls, and every wall has one of four shapes. The shapes are the digits of a base-4 counter. One trip of the head (from the right end and back) adds 1 to that counter: the head runs left over every wall showing digit 3, turning it into digit 0 (a carry), changes the first wall that is not a 3 to its next shape, and comes back. The last wall is the least significant digit.

Each change moves words between the two blocks beside the wall. Over a full cycle of four changes a wall takes 3 words from the block on its left and adds 6 to the block on its right. The left end 10 is one more digit, a binary one: a carry turns it into 00, and the next carry makes the head run to the left end (the visit of the left end) and back, after which every wall shows 0 again. So one period from one visit to the next is 2·4k trips, and over a period the first block loses 4 words, block j loses 12·4j−2 and the last block gains 12·4k−1: the countdown seen in the table above, now derived.

When a block between two walls runs out, the two walls become one wall (1010)r made of r walls with nothing between them. That wall is again a base-4 digit (its four shapes change only at its two ends) with the same totals −3 and +6, so the blocks to its right move one level down and drain four times slower. After every second visit of the left end the right end grows a new wall 1010 with a block of 5 words. All of these rules are proved in Lean for every block length (and every r), in lean/Odometer.lean.

Try it. The panel below runs the counter itself, from the real tape at step 2,973,727, one trip at a time, with the step count of each trip (19, 31, 19 or 4 for each wall that changes, plus 8 steps for each word of every block the head crosses). Running it to the left end gives step 3,477,317 and the tape 00 a45 1 a186 1 a685 1 a407 110, which is exactly what the plain simulation of the machine shows at that step.

sections.heading: The countdown, followed exactly far out
html: Because these rules apply many trips at once in closed form (all walls are digits; a jump stops only where a block gets short, a wall has a shape whose rule is not yet known, or the left end overflows), the run can be followed exactly far beyond any simulation: the macro in py/odometer/ reached step 101520 (1521 digits, given exactly in data/odometer/summary.json) after 8,776 visits of the left end, with 1261 walls on the tape, and no halt. Every trip that is not a plain digit change (a visit of the left end, a new wall, a block running out, walls merging) is run cell by cell on a copy of the tape whose long blocks are cut down to the same length modulo 12, and its step count is corrected by the measured 8 or 19 steps per word. The macro agrees with the plain simulation at every visit of the left end up to 5·1010 steps, step count included.

The run-outs of the first block. The first block counts down by 4 per visit. When it runs out, it and the walls next to it fold into the left end, which shrinks back to 10 over a few visits, and the next block becomes the first one, counting down by 4 again. The slider shows the tape at visits of the left end (the first 60 blocks, bar length on a logarithmic scale; the thin dark lines are the walls, taller for a wall made of more merged walls). Past the start-up, the first block ran out at visits 22 (step about 108), 35 (step about 1011), 37 (step about 1011), 437 (step about 1077), 445 (step about 1078), 8,516 (step about 101476). Each run-out so far folded the same way, and the run went on without a halt. At the end of the run the first block has 104,965 words left, so the next run-out comes about 26,241 visits later.

Halting. The machine halts only when A reads 0 followed by 1 or D reads 1 followed by 1. No digit change, carry, visit of the left end or new wall does that, and every wall shape met so far, (1010)r for r up to 13 and their four phases, is a digit whose rule is known. A halt would need a new local shape: for instance a block running out in a way not seen yet, or two short blocks next to each other. Whether that can ever happen is the remaining question; it is now a question about the list of block lengths and the order in which they run out, not about the machine.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A base-4 odometer: the walls between blocks of 100 are digits (1010, 0, 1110, 1), a trip of the head adds one; per visit of the left end block j loses 12·4^(j−2) words; merged walls are digits too. Exact macro run to 10^1520 steps, no halt; digit rules in Lean.
